page.overview:
Who is Macbeth?

The great Lord Macbeth was born somewhere around the eleventh century in Alba, Scotland to his father Sinel, the former Thane of Glamis, and an unnamed mother. Not much is said in the text about his early life.

When he reached adulthood, Macbeth worked errands in royal and military duties under King Duncan. Due to his skilled talent with a sword and his bloodlust in battles he quickly became a well-known soldier in the King's army, who had gained people's attention by his viscous and victorious way of fighting. As the king's soldier and first cousin, Macbeth was extremely devoted to the king and was considered an esteemed soldier for his noble acts of courage. Because of his loyalty to the country and the monarch, Macbeth was favoured by Duncan, because of this later earning him the title Thane of Cawdor.

In the upcoming prequel: Macdonwald we may get a bit more info on what happened within his early life

As the war ended with Macbeth and [http://shakespeare.wikia.com/wiki/Banquo Banquo]'s slaughter of Macdonwald and capture of the old Thane of Cawdor in the battle near Forres, [http://shakespeare.wikia.com/wiki/Duncan King Duncan] honored Macbeth in high praise. The King sent a scottish nobleman named Ross to deliver the war hero his reward: the Thane of Cawdor's title since its previous holder was to be hanged for treason. Meanwhile, while on their way back to the royal camp in Forres, Macbeth and Banquo wandered onto a heath, where three witches appeared and greeted them with prophecies. They addressed Macbeth first, hailing him as the Thane of Glamis and Cawdor, and that he will become King afterwards, while Banquo was hailed as a father to a line of kings, though he himself would never be one. As the witches disappeared, Ross arrived and presented Macbeth his new title. It became apparent that Macbeth already begun to harbour ambitions of becoming a king, even after Duncan named his oldest son Malcolm III his heir. He stated that the kingship will fall into his lap by luck alone, and that he would not have to take any action to fulfill the witches' last prophecy: “If chance may have me king, why chance may crown me without my stir.” Macbeth became fixated on the prophecy, ignoring Banquo's advice that “oftentimes to win us to our harm these instruments of darkness tell us truths…to betray us in deepest consequence”.
